data.title: Two Lucky Plaza strata shops put up for sale at $11.4m
data.description:
Units may be bought together or separately from $5.7m each. 

Two adjoining freehold strata shops on the ground floor of Lucky Plaza have been put up for sale at a guide price of $11.4m.

The units may be purchased together or separately, with each shop priced from $5.7m, according to marketing agent CBRE.

The guide price translates to about $13,000 psf based on the combined strata area. 

Each unit has a strata area of about 441 square feet and comes with food and beverage approval.

The shops are located near the atrium of Lucky Plaza, a freehold mixed-use development along Orchard Road with a six-storey retail podium.

The sale will be conducted through an Expression of Interest exercise. It will close on Thursday, 15 October.

No Additional Buyer’s Stamp Duty or Seller’s Stamp Duty will apply to the acquisition.

Foreigners and corporate entities are eligible to buy the properties.

data.title: All-Link H1 2026 net profit sinks 19.8% despite revenue jump
data.description:
Malaysia added $3.53m in revenue after the 2025 acquisition.

All-Link Air & Sea Limited’s (All-Link) net profit attributable to owners of the company fell 19.8% year-on-year (YoY) to $2.95m (US$2.32m) in the first half (H1) of 2026.

Revenue rose 38.2% to $50.93m (US$40.1m), driven by organic volume expansion across existing operations and the initial full-period contribution from its Malaysia operations.

The Malaysia operations contributed $3.53m (US$2.78m) following the August 2025 acquisition of MF Logistics Sdn Bhd’s freight forwarding business.

Gross profit rose 28% YoY to $3.01m (US$4.62m), whilst gross profit margin fell 0.9 percentage points (ppt) to 11.5%.

Profit after tax (PAT) decreased 21.4% to (US$2.37m), whilst adjusted PAT grew 11.6% to $4.29m (US$3.38m).

Adjusted net profit margin slipped 2 ppt to 8.4%. Basic and diluted earnings per share were 2.64 Singapore cents (2.08 US cents), down 19.7% YoY from 3.29 Singapore cents (2.59 US cents).

Core freight forwarding services expanded by 34.4% YoY to $47.63m (US$37.5m), representing 93.6% of H1’s total revenue.

Other third-party logistics services surged by 133.2% YoY to $3.26m (US$2.57m) from $1.40m (US$1.10m), driven by heightened demand for cross-border logistics management and value-added warehousing support within the regional e-commerce supply chain.

Other income grew by 66.4% YoY to $0.90m (US$0.71m) from $0.55m (US$0.43m), primarily lifted by a $0.48m (US$0.38m) non-operating gain recognised on the final settlement of contingent purchase consideration for the Malaysia acquisition.

The group’s cash and bank balances stood at $25.27m (US$19.9m) as at 30 June, whilst its SGX Mainboard listing subsequently raised $20.1m in gross proceeds, strengthening its financial position.

It is also advancing its proposed acquisition of a 30% stake in Vietnam ALLLink-TNR International Logistics Co., Ltd., whilst expanding into Thailand and intending to establish a subsidiary in Indonesia.

“Looking ahead, the Group expects a stronger second half, reflecting the seasonal peak in shipment volumes during the key festive periods in the fourth quarter,” All-Link said.

It expects FY2026 revenue to be higher than FY2025, barring unforeseen circumstances.

(US$1 = SG$1.27)

data.title: SG's PathFin.ai AI-sharing programme grows to over 300 participants
data.description:
The initiative aims to lower the cost for smaller financial institutions adopting AI. 

The Monetary Authority of Singapore’s (MAS) PathFin.ai programme to share artificial intelligence (AI) solutions has grown to over 300 participants since its launch in August 2025. 

“Smaller financial institutions can lower the cost and effort of finding and deploying effective AI solutions,” said MAS Managing Director Chia Der Jiun at the Global FinTech Fest 2026 on 11 September.

The programme was previously reported in October to have brought together more than 80 financial institutions to share their experiences and strategies in using AI. 

Its initial use cases covered areas including sales and marketing, customer operations, risk management, and engineering and technology.

“If a solution has been validated and works, we want to make it easier for others to find and implement it,” Chia added.

MAS is also testing AI models with law enforcement and the banking industry, using cross-bank and public-private data to detect suspicious accounts and transactions in near real time. 

“The aim is to detect sooner, intervene faster, and reduce losses,” Chia said. “We expect to have findings from this work by the end of this year.”

data.title: OCBC tops Forbes' 2026 World's Top Performing Banks list
data.description:
DBS takes second place ahead of HDFC Bank and China Merchants Bank.

Singapore’s OCBC ranked first amongst Tier 1 global banks in Forbes’ inaugural World’s Top Performing Banks 2026 list.

DBS placed second in the same category, putting the two Singapore-headquartered lenders ahead of Mumbai’s HDFC Bank, Shenzhen’s China Merchants Bank, and New York’s JPMorganChase.

Tier 1 covers banks with more than $634.5b (US$500b) in total assets. A total of 24 institutions were included in the category.

The ranking, compiled by Forbes in partnership with market research firm Statista, assessed banks using financial data rather than customer survey results.

Banks were evaluated across profitability, capital and funding resilience, asset quality and efficiency, and growth and earnings quality.

Overall, 500 institutions from 89 countries were included in the 2026 ranking.

$1 = US$0.79

data.title: Reclaims Global net profit climbs 53.1% to $3.8m in H1
data.description:
Revenue jumped 52.9% to $33.3m from $21.8m.

Reclaims Global Limited’s net profit jumped 53.1% year-on-year to $3.8m in the first half ended 31 July 2026, up from $2.5m.

Revenue rose 52.9% to $33.3m from $21.8m a year earlier, whilst profit before tax climbed 64.9% to $4.7m from $2.9m.

Excavation Services remained the largest revenue contributor, increasing 47.3% to $24.1m from $16.4m.

Revenue from Logistics and Leasing grew 52% to $7.2m from $4.8m, whilst Recycling revenue surged 171.9% to $1.7m from $600,000.

Higher business volumes also lifted the group’s costs, including materials, services, and consumables as well as employee expenses.

Reclaims Global said it was more selective in bidding for new projects during the first quarter amidst volatile energy prices. 

Higher diesel costs were factored in for later tenders, it added.

The group completed two freehold property investments during the half, including the $35.1m acquisition of Lasidon Holdings Pte. Ltd., which owns a commercial property at 291 Serangoon Road. 

It also bought an industrial property at 464 Tagore Industrial Avenue for $20.5m.

Reclaims Global declared an interim dividend of 0.25 cents per share.

data.title: Tokyo Court rejects IHH unit's claims against Daiichi Sankyo
data.description:
NTK weighs legal options after ruling on case linked to Fortis tender offer delays.

Northern TK Venture Pte Ltd (NTK), an indirect wholly owned subsidiary of IHH Healthcare, had all its claims against Daiichi Sankyo Co. Ltd. dismissed by the Tokyo District Court on 10 September. 

In addition, the court ordered the company to bear the litigation costs, according to a bourse filing.

NTK said it disagrees with the decision and is reviewing the judgment with its legal counsel.

It is also evaluating available legal remedies and intends to continue pursuing the relief sought in the case.

The dispute relates to IHH’s 2018 acquisition of Fortis Healthcare in India.

IHH said it suffered losses after delays in obtaining approvals needed for the mandatory tender offer connected with the acquisition. 

The delays occurred amidst a dispute between Daiichi Sankyo and its judgment debtors, to which it was not a party, the group added.

IHH-NTK acquired Fortis through a preferential allotment of newly issued shares worth $535.4m (INR40b), alongside a mandatory tender offer to public shareholders.

The transaction secured the required corporate, shareholder and regulatory approvals.

IHH said it did not acquire secondary shares from Fortis’ former promoters and made no payments to them as part of the transaction.

$1 = INR74.71

data.title: Building owners urged to provide dedicated bays for delivery riders
data.description:
New LTA-URA guide also recommends 15-minute parking grace periods and simpler entry. 

Building owners and managers are encouraged to provide dedicated waiting bays for delivery riders using motorcycles, bicycles and power-assisted bicycles under new guidelines from the Land Transport Authority and Urban Redevelopment Authority (URA).

The guide recommends locating delivery waiting bays near entrances, lift lobbies, escalators, and food and beverage outlets.

Bays should be separated by vehicle type and kept away from vehicular access points, fire engine access routes, and fire escape routes.

Motorcycles are recommended to be given spaces measuring about 0.8 metres by 2.4 metres each, whilst bicycles and power-assisted bicycles should have about 0.7 metres by 1.8 metres.

The recommendation is part of the new Last-Mile Delivery Guide for developers, architects, building managers and Management Corporation Strata Title councils.

URA and the National Delivery Champions Association have also worked with the Singapore Land Authority to publish delivery waiting-bay locations on OneMap. Building owners can submit new or unmapped bays for inclusion.

Building managers are also encouraged to offer delivery riders a parking grace period of at least 15 minutes. URA and Housing and Development Board car parks already offer a 15-minute grace period.

Other recommendations include simplifying security registration through building management apps, setting up parcel or food lockers near entrances, and allowing residents and tenants to collect deliveries at ground-floor lobbies.

For MCST developments, the guide says access for delivery personnel and their vehicles is already required under the Building Maintenance and Strata Management Act.

It also calls for adequate lift capacity and access for delivery personnel.

“Delivery personnel provided feedback that poor lift design and practices can add 10 to 15 minutes per delivery, cutting into earnings and causing delivery personnel to avoid certain developments,” it said.

Developments are also advised to improve signage, lighting and network connectivity in common areas and basement car parks, with Wi-Fi suggested where mobile coverage is poor.

data.title: Singapore captures 91.7% of Southeast Asia robotics funding
data.description:
Most of the total regional investment came from a single funding round.

Singapore accounted for 91.7% of Southeast Asia’s all-time robotics funding, according to a report from private-market data platform Tracxn.

Robotics companies in the city-state raised $986m across 58 funding rounds.

Singapore was home to 108 of the 242 robotics companies tracked across the region. Of these, 37 had secured institutional funding.

The city-state’s most-funded robotics companies were Sharpa, which raised $670m, followed by Fourier Intelligence with $83m and Neptune Robotics with $69.5m.

Across Southeast Asia, robotics companies raised $1.1b in all-time equity funding. Only 51 of the 242 tracked companies had received institutional investment.

Annual funding reached a record $696m in 2026 year to date, rising from $52m in 2025 and $10.2m in 2021.

However, the increase was driven primarily by Sharpa’s $670m Series D round in August. The transaction accounted for most of the year’s funding and exceeded the sector’s combined investment before 2026.

Deal activity remained limited, with six funding rounds recorded in 2026 year to date, compared with three in 2025 and 10 in 2021.

The sector also remained concentrated at the early stages. Only 22 companies had reached Series A or later, whilst nine had reached Series B, five had reached Series C and three had reached Series D or beyond.

No Southeast Asian robotics company had achieved unicorn status or completed an initial public offering.

The region recorded only one acquisition: Light Ray Holdings’ purchase of kitchen robotics company Zimplistic, which developed Rotimatic, in October 2020. The acquisition price was not disclosed.

data.title: Monday Wrap: Fusion timelines, healthcare gaps, credit surge
data.description:
Experts debate fusion's timeline as shifting healthcare, retail, and credit trends reframe the domestic outlook.

Last week in Singapore Business Review, experts offered sharply different timelines for when fusion energy could contribute to Singapore’s electricity supply as AI-driven growth raises power demand. Platform workers gained access to lower-cost healthcare through a new private-sector programme, whilst routine outpatient care remains outside statutory protections. Singapore’s buildings are increasingly combining different uses, retail growth slowed as shoppers became more cautious, and loan growth reached its fastest pace since 2014.

Singapore’s push to support AI-driven growth is putting fusion power in the spotlight, but experts disagree by decades on when the technology could contribute to the city-state’s electricity supply. MTI raised its 2026 growth forecast to 4.5% to 5.5% on 11 August, citing stronger global spending on AI. The stronger economy is expected to lift electricity demand, whilst Singapore relies almost entirely on imported fuel, has limited land for renewable energy and faces growing power needs from data centres.

The timeline for fusion remains uncertain. Industry projections point to possible commercial deployment in the mid-2030s, whilst independent analysis puts a meaningful role much further out, potentially beyond 2050. 

Focused Energy CEO Thomas Forner sees Singapore as a potential hub and off-taker, with a possible prototype plant in 2035, whilst NTU professor Xavier Garbet described deployment in the 2030s as ambitious and uncertain. Wood Mackenzie’s Prakash Sharma sees a meaningful opportunity only after 2050.

Singapore is also positioning itself in the sector. Commonwealth Fusion Systems signed a research agreement with A*STAR in May focused on technologies for commercial fusion power plants, whilst its CEO identified Singapore as a potential fusion hub. The experts, however, highlighted continuing challenges around technology, materials, regulation, supply chains and commercialisation.

For platform workers, the introduction of RiderCare by foodpanda and Singlife provides lower-cost access to healthcare, but does not change the coverage provided under the Platform Workers Act. The Act provides work injury protections, CPF contributions and representation rights, but routine outpatient medical care is not covered. Work injury protection applies to medical expenses and income losses linked to work accidents rather than unrelated illness or treatment.

MOM counted 71,600 regular platform workers in 2025, including 14,700 delivery workers. Meanwhile, WTW expects medical costs in Singapore to rise 16.9% in 2026, up from 15.5% last year. Singlife’s 2025 report found that 60% of platform workers cited healthcare costs as a concern, compared with 45% of non-platform workers.

Singapore’s buildings are also increasingly combining residential, healthcare, workplace, community and transport functions as projects seek to make better use of limited land. Siah Puay Lin, Singapore lead at SJ Group, said transport-oriented and mixed-use projects are changing how urban density is planned, with connected and walkable precincts integrating residential, healthcare, wellness and community uses.

Examples include Geneo at 1 and 7 Science Park Drive and Bulim Square, which are reworking industrial and business park formats with additional amenities. In healthcare, CPG’s Chung Yen Ling said demand is growing across acute hospitals, facility renewal, mental healthcare and community-based long-term care, with projects including Eastern General Hospital, NUH redevelopment and several care homes.

The rollout of CORENET X is also changing how projects are coordinated. The national building regulatory submission platform uses building information modelling, with mandatory adoption for projects of at least 30,000 square metres of gross floor area from October 2025 and upcoming projects from October 2026. Siah said BIM can improve coordination and reduce revisions during construction.

Retail sales rose 1.5% year on year in July, down from 4% in June, whilst seasonally adjusted sales increased 0.9% month on month. UOB attributed the weaker performance to cautious consumer sentiment amidst a softer labour market.

Retrenchments rose to 4,500 in the second quarter from 3,830 in the first quarter, whilst a Singapore National Employers Federation survey found 54% of employers did not expect to increase headcount in 2027. RHB expects retail momentum to moderate in the second half of the year, with full-year growth forecast at 3% and second-half growth at around 2% year on year.

Some categories continued to perform strongly. Recreational goods sales rose 13.9% in July, whilst watches and jewellery increased 11.1%. Department stores, however, recorded their sixth decline in seven months. RHB expects essentials to remain more resilient whilst discretionary categories face greater exposure to higher living costs and more cautious spending.

Singapore’s loans and advances rose 12.5% year on year in July, up from 11.7% in June and marking the fastest growth since 2014, according to MAS data. Nomura said corporate loan growth was broad-based at 13.4%, led by financial services and insurance, manufacturing, general commerce and transport.

Consumer loans rose 10.4%, driven by car loans, credit cards and share financing, whilst mortgages continued to improve. Nomura said financial conditions remained supportive of growth, although the credit gap had moved into territory comparable with previous periods of strong expansion.

Liquidity has also begun to tighten. The loan-to-deposit ratio rose to 70.3% in July from 67.7% at the end of 2025, whilst deposit growth slowed to 5.3% year on year from 7.6% in June. Nomura expects domestic rates to move higher alongside the maturing credit cycle and forecasts 2026 core inflation at 2.1%.
